title: Gilgamish washes and dresses
short: The victorious Gilgamish washes, loosens his hair and puts on clean clothes and a crown: his beauty attracts Ishtar.
body: Washing and dressing mark a change of status in the poem: Enkidu became human by grooming (II), and Gilgamish's return to civilised life is again marked by bathing and a new garment (XI). Thompson's note explains that he uses the historic present here. The 'fillet' is a headband or crown, a sign of kingship. His beauty in his clean robes is what provokes Ishtar's desire, so the washing scene sets the episode in motion.

title: Ishtar's proposal
short: Ishtar asks Gilgamish to be her husband, promising a golden chariot and fertile flocks: the language of a sacred marriage.
body: Mesopotamian kings sometimes celebrated a ritual 'sacred marriage' with Inanna/Ishtar, and the goddess's offer echoes that royal ideology: she promises tribute from kings and fertility for his herds. Gilgamish's refusal is unexpected for a king and has been read as the hero's rejection of the goddess's fatal love, or as hubris. Her promise that he will enter 'our house with the fragrance of cedar' ties the episode to the Cedar Forest just completed.

title: 'Azure': lapis lazuli
short: Thompson's 'azure' translates uqnu, lapis lazuli, the deep-blue stone from Afghanistan prized above all others in Mesopotamia.
body: Lapis lazuli and gold were the luxury materials par excellence, used for divine statues and royal jewellery. Thompson consistently renders uqnu as 'azure' (the colour) or 'sapphire' (XI); modern translators say 'lapis lazuli'. The same stone forms the tablet on which Gilgamish's story is written in the prologue (in George's text), the bowl in the funeral rites (VIII), the jewelled garden (IX) and the 'flies' of the mother-goddess (XI). Thompson's note glosses another gem in the line (elmesu) as uncertain.

title: Gilgamish's catalogue of insults
short: Gilgamish refuses Ishtar with a string of metaphors: a ruin, a back door, a leaking waterskin, a shoe that bites.
body: The images are domestic and proverbial: each is something useful that fails its owner (pitch that soils, a waterskin that soaks, limestone that weakens a wall, an amulet that fails abroad). Thompson's note explains the chalcedony as a seal-cylinder or amulet. The speech is one of the most rhetorically elaborate in the epic and shows the hero's new confidence. It is also dangerous: insulting a great goddess has consequences.

title: Tammuz (Dumuzi) and the Wailing
short: Tammuz, Ishtar's young husband, died and was mourned every year: his fate heads the list of her ruined lovers.
body: Thompson explains the yearly Wailing for Tammuz, who dies in autumn and is brought back in spring. In Sumerian myth Dumuzi is handed over to the underworld in Inanna's place (Descent of Inanna). The cult reached Jerusalem: Ezekiel 8:14 describes 'women weeping for Tammuz' at the temple gate. Gilgamish's point is that Ishtar's love leads to death. The lament for Dumuzi was a public ritual in Mesopotamia, performed by women in the summer month that bore his name.

title: The Roller bird and its cry 'kappi'
short: Ishtar broke the wing of the allallu-bird, which now cries 'kappi!', 'my wing!': a myth explaining a bird's call.
body: Thompson identifies the bird as the roller, a brightly coloured bird of the palm-groves whose tumbling flight may lie behind the legend. The cry kappi means 'my wing' in Akkadian, an onomatopoeic pun. Like the other lovers (lion, stallion, shepherd, gardener), the bird is a victim of Ishtar's changeable love, the series moving from animals to humans. The bird's broken wing is a picture of maimed love.

title: The Stallion and his mother Silili
short: The stallion Ishtar loved was given the whip and spur; his mother Silili, a divine mare, mourns him.
body: The horse's fate is the fate of all domesticated animals: harnessed, forced to gallop, made to drink muddy water. Silili is the mother of horses. The 'fifty miles' renders a distance of seven leagues in George's text. Thompson notes that a Boghazköy fragment lists horses among Ishtar's gifts. Ishtar's lovers are described in terms that recall the treatment of real domestic animals: bridled, spurred and driven. The point of the catalogue is cumulative: every creature she loved was diminished or destroyed, and Gilgamish fears the same fate. The mother's lament adds a note of pathos to the stallion's story.

title: The Shepherd turned into a wolf
short: The herdsman who gave Ishtar daily offerings was turned into a beast and chased by his own dogs; George reads 'wolf', Thompson 'jackal'.
body: The animal word barbaru is usually translated 'wolf' today. The story has been compared with the Greek myth of Actaeon, hunted by his own dogs after offending Artemis. The shepherd's offerings of baked bread and kids recall real temple offerings, so his fate suggests that even piety does not protect the goddess's lover. Transformation of a lover into an animal is a common motif of myth, and here it shows the goddess's power over the boundary between human and beast, the very boundary Enkidu crossed in the other direction.

title: Ishullanu, the gardener
short: Ishullanu, Anu's date-gardener, rejected Ishtar and was transformed into a creature whose name (dallalu) is obscure: Thompson guesses 'spider'.
body: He alone refuses the goddess, and his reply (that he eats only what his mother bakes) mocks her offer; Thompson's note calls it hard to translate. The transformed creature is dallalu, 'an unknown word, perhaps lit. the spinner'. Modern translators treat the creature's identity as uncertain. The episode is the climax of the list, because Ishullanu, like Gilgamish, refuses her.

title: Anu and Antu, Ishtar's parents
short: Ishtar goes to heaven to complain to her father Anu and her mother Antu, like an insulted daughter.
body: Antu is Anu's consort. Making Ishtar the child of Anu reflects the Uruk tradition, where they shared the Eanna temple. The scene is almost comic: the furious goddess runs to her parents, and Anu points out that she started it. Anu's reply, that Gilgamish has only told the truth, shows the father's reluctance. Ishtar then threatens to break open the underworld and let the dead devour the living, a threat that Thompson restores from the Descent of Ishtar. Anu yields, but only after warning her about the famine the Bull will cause. The scene thus prepares the Bull of Heaven and shows the domestic politics of the gods.

title: The Bull of Heaven
short: Ishtar demands the Bull of Heaven to destroy Gilgamish; its snorts open pits that swallow hundreds of men.
body: The Bull of Heaven (Sumerian Gud-anna) is a cosmic beast, possibly connected with the constellation Taurus, as some scholars have argued. Ishtar threatens to raise the dead to eat the living unless Anu agrees, a threat that Thompson says is usually restored from the Descent of Ishtar. The heroes' killing of the bull is their second great exploit and the final provocation: the gods now decide on Enkidu's death.

title: Seven years of famine
short: Anu warns that the Bull will bring seven years of empty husks; Ishtar claims to have stored grain and fodder.
body: The Bull is a figure of drought and famine. The motif of seven lean years and stored grain invites comparison with Joseph and Pharaoh's dream in Genesis 41. The exchange shows Anu's concern for mankind and Ishtar's readiness to destroy for revenge, anticipating her role in the Flood (XI). The motif also shows that divine anger has consequences for the whole land, not only for the offending hero.

title: The killing of the Bull
short: Enkidu seizes the Bull by the horns and tail while Gilgamish thrusts his sword between its neck and horns.
body: George's fuller text describes the teamwork: Enkidu holds the bull by its tail, and Gilgamish kills it like a butcher. Bull-wrestling scenes are common in Mesopotamian seal art. The friends then offer its heart to Shamash, turning the kill into a sacrifice. In Thompson's broken text Enkidu does most of the work; in fuller versions the two friends cooperate, as they had against Humbaba. The scene is a deliberate counterpart to the Humbaba fight: a monster of the earth and a monster of heaven. Some interpreters connect the Bull's killing with the constellation Taurus, though this remains speculative.

title: The heart offered to Shamash
short: The heroes offer the Bull's heart to Shamash and sit down as 'the two brothers'.
body: Offering the heart, the seat of life, to the god who protects them reasserts their bond with Shamash. The phrase 'the two brothers' sums up the friendship at its height, just before Enkidu's fall. Their sacrifice of the heart parallels their offerings to Shamash before the Cedar Forest journey (III). By placing the slaughter under the Sun-god's protection, the heroes treat the killing as justified, but Ishtar and Enlil will see it differently. The tranquil image of the 'brothers' sitting down together is the last such picture before the gods' sentence.

title: Enkidu's insult to Ishtar
short: Enkidu tears off part of the Bull and throws it at Ishtar: Thompson's 'member' suggests the genitals, but George reads imittu, 'haunch'.
body: The word imittu means the right thigh or haunch of an animal, a standard cut of meat. Thompson understood an obscene gesture, an interpretation that fits the following lament by Ishtar's women 'over the member'. George's reading keeps the insult (throwing a joint of meat at a goddess) but removes the sexual sense. Either way the act is the worst blasphemy in the epic and seals Enkidu's fate.

title: Ishtar's women
short: Ishtar gathers three classes of women attached to her cult, kezretu, samhatu and harimatu, to lament over the Bull.
body: Thompson's 'girl-devotees, the hetaerae and harlots' renders three Akkadian terms whose exact meaning is debated; all denote women associated with Ishtar's cult and with sexuality. The second, samhatu, is the same word as the courtesan's name Shamhat in Tablet I. Their ritual lament over the Bull mirrors the lament for Tammuz. Thompson uses three different English terms to keep the distinction. Their lament gives the scene the shape of a funeral rite.

title: The horns dedicated to Lugal-banda
short: The Bull's huge horns, each holding six measures of oil, are hung in Lugal-banda's shrine as oil vessels.
body: Votive gifts of trophies in temples were common. Dedicating the horns to his father's god also shows the hero's family piety. The craftsmen's admiration for the horns' size echoes the craftsmen of Tablet III. The horns are said to be of lapis lazuli, each weighing thirty minas, and the craftsmen of the city gather to admire them, as they had gathered to forge the weapons of Tablet III. Gilgamish hangs them in his family shrine, where they serve as vessels for anointing oil, so the triumph is converted into an act of ancestral piety.

title: The Euphrates
short: The Euphrates was the river of Uruk; the friends wash their hands in it before riding in triumph through the city.
body: Uruk stood on a branch of the Euphrates in antiquity. Washing hands after killing is purification. Shuruppak, the Flood city, also lies on its bank (XI). The river was the lifeline of southern Mesopotamia, and many cities stood on its banks. In George's text the Cedar Forest timber has also been floated down the Euphrates to Nippur (Tablet V). Washing in the river after the slaughter marks the end of the deed and the return to the city, where the heroes ride in triumph through the streets.

title: The triumph song
short: Gilgamish asks the women of Uruk who is the finest of heroes and answers himself: the peak of his pride.
body: Thompson calls it a riddle; in George's text it is a call-and-response song sung by the palace women. The scene is the high point of the heroes' glory and pride, immediately followed by Enkidu's ominous dream. Its placement at the centre of the twelve tablets marks the turning of the poem from triumph to grief. The structure of question and answer suggests a real song of praise.
